Jehoram
jeh-HOR-am
proper noun (a king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat)
Hebrew Yehoram, “the LORD is exalted,” from Yeho-, a shortened form of the covenant name, and ram, high or exalted. Not to be confused with his brother-in-law and contemporary Joram, king of Israel and son of Ahab (see the separate entry).

Biblical Definition

Jehoram was the son of the godly Jehoshaphat and became king of Judah in his father’s stead, but he did not walk in his father’s way. He had married Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, and through that marriage he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab (2Ki 8:18). His first recorded act as king was to secure his throne by murder: he rose up to the kingdom of his father, strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword, and divers also of the princes of Israel (2Ch 21:4). His reign of eight years brought Edom and Libnah into revolt, and Elijah sent him a written prophecy of disease and disaster for having made Judah to go a whoring, and forcing Judah thereto. That judgment fell exactly: he died of an incurable bowel disease, and his people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers. He departed without being desired, and though buried in the city of David, it was not in the sepulchres of the kings (2Ch 21:20). Scripture makes his contrast with his father explicit and deliberate: a covenant heir, married into an idolatrous house, undoing in one generation what a godly father had labored to build.

Webster 1828 Definition

A king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, who married Athaliah of the house of Ahab and led Judah into apostasy; died unlamented and unburied among the kings.

expand to see more

JEHORAM, n. A king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat and husband of Athaliah, daughter of Ahab.

He murdered his brothers to secure his throne upon his accession.

He walked in the way of the kings of Israel through his marriage into Ahab’s house.

He received written judgment from Elijah and died of a grievous disease.

He was buried in the city of David, but not among the sepulchres of the kings.

Key Scripture

2Ki 8:16 — "And in the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign."

2Ki 8:18 — "And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: for the daughter of Ahab was his wife: and he did evil in the sight of the LORD."

2Ch 21:4 — "Now when Jehoram was risen up to the kingdom of his father, he strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword, and divers also of the princes of Israel."

2Ch 21:20 — "Thirty and two years old was he when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years, and departed without being desired. Howbeit they buried him in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings."

Modern Corruption

No modern movement has redefined Jehoram; the principle his life fixes — that marriage into an ungodly house can undo a generation of covenant faithfulness — is simply ignored rather than argued against.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jehoram is not a contested figure; he is a largely forgotten one, which is its own kind of loss, since the pattern his reign fixes is exactly the pattern many households still walk into with open eyes.

The principle to recover is the force of 2 Chronicles 21’s own verdict: he was Jehoshaphat’s son, raised under a reforming, covenant-keeping king, yet the daughter of Ahab was his wife, and by that single alliance the way of the kings of Israel entered Judah’s throne. Scripture does not blame Jehoram’s apostasy on ignorance or on distant ancestry; it names the marriage as the hinge. A household’s covenant faithfulness is not self-perpetuating by pedigree alone; it is a trust that can be undone within a single generation by exactly the alliance Jehoram made, and the text’s closing detail — buried, but not among the kings, departed without being desired — is Scripture’s own judgment on where that road ends.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yehoram, “the LORD is exalted,” a name shared with his Israelite counterpart Joram, whom Scripture and later usage distinguish by the fuller form Jehoram for the king of Judah.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yeho- — a shortened form of the covenant name YHWH, prefixed to many royal Judahite names.

Hebrew ram — high, exalted, lifted up; the root shared with words for height and pride.

2 Kings 8:16 names him son of Jehoshaphat, distinguishing him at once from Joram son of Ahab in the same verse.

2 Chronicles 21 supplies the fullest and most severe account of his reign, including Elijah’s written prophecy against him.

His marriage to Athaliah later brought the house of David to the brink of extinction under her own usurpation (2 Kings 11).

Usage

"“He walked in the way of the kings of Israel... for the daughter of Ahab was his wife” — the hinge of his apostasy."

"“He strengthened himself, and slew all his brethren with the sword” — his first act as king."

"“He departed without being desired” — Scripture’s verdict on his death."
